source_text: His compressi erumpunt dicere: (sufficit unicum hoc opus deo nostro, quod hominem liberauit summa et praecipua bonitate sua et omnibus locustis anteponenda\'. o deum maiorem, cuius tam magnum opus non potuit inueniri quam in homine dei minoris! enimuero prius est, ut eum probes esse per quae deum probari oportet, per opera, tunc deinde per beneficia. primo enim quaeritur, an sit, et ita, qualis sit. alterum de operibus, alterum de beneficiis dinoscetur. ceterum non quia liberasse dicitur hominem, ideo esse eum constat, sed si esse constiterit, tunc et liberasse dicetur, ut et an liberauerit constet, quia potuerit et esse et non liberasse. quomodo ergo, quia liberasse dicetur, etiam esse credetur, cum potuerit et esse et non liberasse? . Nunc, in isto articulo ab ignoti dei quaestione deducto si satis constitit tam nihil illum condidisse quam debuisse condidisse, uti cognosceretur ex operibus, quia si fuisset, cognosci debuisset, et utique a primordio rerum, — deum enim non decuisset latuisse — regrediar necesse est ad originem quaestionis dei ignoti, ut ceteros quoque ramulos eius excutiam. primo enim quaeri oportebit, qui postea se protulerit in notitiam cur postea et non a primordio rerum quibus utique necessarius, qua deus, et quidem necessarior quo melior latere non debuit. non enim potest dici non fuisse aut materiam aut causam cognoscendi deum, cum et homo a primordio esset in saeculo, cui nunc subuenit, et malitia creatoris, aduersus quam ut bonus subuenit. igitur aut ignorauit et causam et materiam suae reuelationis necessariae aut dubitanit ++ aut non potuit aut noluit. omnia haec deo indigna, maxime optimo. sed et hunc locum alibi implebimus exprobratione serae reuelationis, sicut nunc sola demonstratione.
pass_a_gloss: These compressed ones burst forth to say: it suffices for our God this one work, that He freed man by His supreme and principal goodness, and to be preferred to all locusts. O greater God, whose so great work could not be found except in the man of the lesser God! For indeed, first it is necessary to prove Him to be through those things by which God ought to be proven, through works, then afterwards through benefits. For first it is sought, whether He is, and thus, what kind He is. One thing will be discerned from works, another from benefits. Moreover, not because it is said that He freed man, therefore it is established that He is, but if it is established that He is, then it will also be said that He freed, so that it may also be established whether He freed, because He was able both to be and not to free. How therefore, because it will be said that He freed, is it also believed that He is, when He was able both to be and not to free? Now, in this article, having been drawn away from the question of the unknown God, if it is sufficiently established that He neither created to the same extent as He ought to have created, so that He might be known from works, because if He had been, He ought to have been known, and certainly from the beginning of things, — for it was not fitting for God to have been hidden — I must return to the origin of the question of the unknown God, so that I may also shake off the other branches of it. For first it will be necessary to ask, He who afterwards presented Himself to notice, why afterwards and not from the beginning of things, for which, since He is God, He was certainly necessary, and how much more necessary, the better He is, it was not fitting to hide. For it cannot be said that there was not a material or cause for knowing God, since man was also in the world from the beginning, to whom He now comes to aid, and the malice of the creator, against which, as good, He comes to aid. Therefore, either He ignored and the cause and material of His necessary revelation, or He doubted, or He was not able, or He did not wish. All these things are unworthy of God, especially the best. But also we will fill this place elsewhere with the reproach of the late revelation, just as now with the sole demonstration.

pass_b_english: My opponents burst out, tight-lipped and sputtering: "This one deed is enough for our God — He freed humanity by His supreme and principal goodness, a deed worth more than all the locusts in Egypt." Oh, what a greater God, whose mightiest work cannot be found except in the man of the lesser God! But the order of proof is backwards. You must first establish that He exists by the standard that proves any God: His works. Only then do you weigh His benefits. The first question is always whether He exists, and if so, what He is like. Works answer the first; benefits answer the second. The mere claim that He freed humanity does not prove He exists. Existence must be settled first; only then can we ask whether He actually freed anyone — because a being who exists could always have chosen not to liberate. So how does the claim that He freed Him become grounds for believing He exists, when He could just as well have existed and done nothing?

Now, since this argument has dragged us away from the question of the unknown God, let us grant for the moment that it has been sufficiently established: He did not create to the same degree that He ought to have created, so that He might be known through His works. If He had existed, He ought to have been known — and from the very beginning of things, for it was not fitting for God to remain hidden. I must therefore return to the root of the question of the unknown God, so that I can shake loose its other branches as well. First we must ask: the One who only later revealed Himself — why only later, and not from the beginning of the very things for which, as God, He was absolutely necessary? And the better He is, the more necessary He was; He had no business staying hidden. It cannot be said that there was no material or cause for knowing God. Humanity existed in the world from the beginning — the very humanity He now comes to aid — and the malice of the Creator existed from the beginning, against which, as good, He now comes to aid. So either He ignored both the cause and the material for His own necessary revelation, or He hesitated, or He was unable, or He was unwilling. Every one of these options is unworthy of God, especially the best God. We will take up the indictment of His late revelation elsewhere; for now, the demonstration alone must suffice.

review.notes: Pass A contains a significant mistranslation of 'locustis' (locusts) which is likely an OCR error for 'locis' (places) in the source, but Pass B introduces a massive hallucination/addition by interpreting it as 'locusts in Egypt' (the phrase 'locusts in Egypt' does not appear in the Latin source). Additionally, Pass A fails to translate 'tam nihil illum condidisse quam debuisse condidisse' accurately, rendering it as 'He neither created to the same extent as He ought to have created', which obscures the comparative sense of the Latin 'tam nihil... quam' (so little... as).
uncertainties: locustis vs locis: The Latin 'locustis' (locusts) is almost certainly an OCR error for 'locis' (places), but the translator must handle the text as provided or note the error. Pass A follows the literal (erroneous) text, while Pass B adds 'in Egypt' which is not in the source.
reasons: Pass B adds 'in Egypt' to the phrase 'locusts in Egypt' which is not present in the Locked Latin 'omnibus locustis anteponenda'.

Pass A's translation of 'tam nihil illum condidisse quam debuisse condidisse' as 'He neither created to the same extent as He ought to have created' is a poor rendering of the comparative 'so little [that He created] as He ought to have created'.

review.notes: The Latin text is correctly translated in both Pass A and Pass B. The title 'God's Creation and Revelation' accurately reflects the content. All lemmas and choices are correctly interpreted. No errors in source identity, completeness, negation, agency, modality, doctrine, or scripture are found. The translation preserves the original meaning and structure of the Latin text.
